title: Why Indian homes are finally embracing the art of the small detail
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
The era of the statement chandelier is giving way to something more quietly radical — the rise of the curated everyday object. For decades, "decorating your home" in India meant one of two things: a major renovation or doing nothing at all. The middle path — upgrading your space incrementally, deliberately, with small but perfectly chosen objects — was simply not available. The market didn't offer it. The culture didn't celebrate it. That is changing.

## The shift we're seeing

Walk into any mid-market apartment in Bengaluru, Pune, or Delhi today and you'll notice something different. The bathroom has a matching set — soap dispenser, toothbrush holder, tray, all in the same material and tone. The kitchen counter has been cleared of accumulated clutter and replaced with two or three purposeful pieces: a chopping board beautiful enough to leave out, a spice rack that earns its counter space. No architect was involved. No lakhs were spent. And yet these spaces feel curated, considered, alive.

## Why it took so long

The answer lies in how the Indian home décor market was structured. At the top: luxury brands with beautiful catalogues aimed at the wealthiest 10%. At the bottom: uncoordinated, purely functional items from local markets and e-commerce mass listings. No one was making design-led, coordinated, affordable home accessories for the vast middle — the family in a 2BHK in Noida or a 1BHK in Thane who cares deeply about their home but cannot justify ₹15,000 for a side table.

## What we believe

Urban Nest was built precisely for this gap. Our belief is simple: every Indian home deserves objects that are beautiful, functional, and designed to work together — not one perfect showpiece, but a coherent, considered home environment you enjoy living in every day. The art of the small detail isn't about minimalism or Instagram aesthetics. It is about choosing the seven things in your bathroom intentionally rather than accumulating twenty things accidentally. The quiet pleasure of a kitchen counter where everything has a place and a purpose. That, to us, is what home really means.

title: Space planning — the hidden science behind a beautiful room
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
When we think about what makes a room feel premium, we reach for obvious answers — expensive furniture, imported fabrics, designer lighting. But visit enough well-designed spaces and a pattern emerges: the rooms that feel truly special have something simpler in common. They are planned well. Space planning is the discipline that determines how furniture, movement, light, and activity are distributed across a room. It is the skeleton beneath the decoration, separating a room that merely contains furniture from one that genuinely functions as a space for human living.

## The three principles that matter

*Movement first.* A room should allow its occupants to move through it comfortably without weaving between chairs. The primary pathway through any space should be clear. This sounds obvious but is routinely ignored — most Indian homes have too much furniture pushed against walls, leaving an awkward void in the centre.

*Zoning.* Even a small room can contain multiple zones — a reading nook, a conversation area, a workspace — if they are defined correctly. The tools are simple: a rug, a change in lighting, the angle of a chair. No walls required.

*Balance, not symmetry.* The goal is visual equilibrium, not mirror-image layouts. A heavy sofa can be balanced by a cluster of smaller furniture on the opposite side. An asymmetric arrangement often feels more alive than a perfectly symmetrical one.

## For Indian homes specifically

Indian interiors often have to solve a unique challenge: multi-purpose spaces where one room serves simultaneously as living room, dining room, and home office. The answer is not to buy less furniture — it is to choose pieces that do multiple jobs and arrange them to create a sense of transition between functions. A well-placed bookshelf can divide a space without a wall. A dining table at the right height serves as a workspace during the day. Space planning turns constraints into design decisions.

title: India's interiors are going soft — and it's perfect
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
For most of the past decade, the dominant aesthetic in Indian urban homes was a fairly literal interpretation of contemporary minimalism: hard lines, rectangular furniture, flat surfaces. It was clean and legible. It was also, if we're honest, a little cold. Something has shifted. The curves are back. Across the country's most interesting new interiors — apartments in Worli, concept cafés in Indiranagar, the mood boards of every designer worth following — organic forms are arriving. Arched doorways. Rounded sofas. Circular rugs. Sculptural accent chairs that look more like abstract art than furniture. This is not a passing trend. It is a correction.

## Why soft geometry works

The science is straightforward: rounded forms trigger a physiological response of comfort and safety. Sharp corners signal alertness; curves signal ease. A sofa with gently rounded arms feels welcoming in a way that a right-angled sectional simply does not. For homes — spaces designed for rest, for the private self — this matters enormously.

## India's relationship with the curve

What makes this trend particularly resonant in the Indian context is that curves are not foreign to Indian design — they are native to it. The arched niches of Rajasthani havelis. The gentle jharokha window-bays of Gujarati architecture. The rounded motifs of classical Indian textiles. Organic form is woven into India's design DNA; it simply got suppressed by a century of modernist influence. The return of curves in contemporary Indian interiors is less a trend import than a homecoming.

## How to start

You don't need to renovate to introduce softness. A single rounded accent chair. A curved mirror. A circular dining table instead of a rectangular one. An arched bookshelf insert. The entry point is lower than you think, and the effect on a room's atmosphere is immediate.

title: What celebrity homes actually teach us about design
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
Glossy home tours of celebrity penthouses tend to generate a predictable response — initial awe at the scale, then the comfortable dismissal: "It's easy to have a beautiful home when you have that kind of money." This dismissal misses the more interesting lesson available in these spaces. The budget is irrelevant. The principle is not.

## Personality as design brief

The most striking thing about any well-curated home — celebrity or otherwise — is the consistency of personality across the entire space. A good home tells you something specific and true about the person who lives in it. When a space is curated around an actual vision, you can feel it. When it is decorated by accumulation — one sofa from here, a gifted artwork from there, a rug that was on sale — you can feel that too. The lesson from these home tours is not "spend more." It is: know what you're trying to say, and let that guide every decision.

## Translated for the rest of us

This kind of intentionality is available to every home, at every budget. It begins with a simple question: what do I actually want to feel when I walk into this room? Not "what looks good on Instagram." Not "what will impress guests." What do I — specifically — want to feel? From that answer, every subsequent decision becomes clearer. You discover you don't need more objects; you need fewer, better-chosen ones. You stop buying what's available and start waiting for what's right. The celebrity penthouse is a useful mirror — not because it shows you what to buy, but because it shows you what a deliberate home looks like.

title: The retro revival — why nostalgia is the hottest design language
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
When Italian architect Fabio Fantolino designed the Lève Office Bar in Turin, he reached backwards — to the 1960s, to Space Age modernism, to the chrome-and-cantilever aesthetic of mid-century Italian offices — and found in that archive something more contemporary than anything designed this decade. Wood panelling, mirror-clad surfaces, cantilever chairs in tubular steel, olive green countertops. An interior simultaneously deeply historical and unmistakably fresh. This is the paradox at the heart of the retro revival: nostalgia, executed well, does not look old. It looks timeless.

## Why vintage aesthetics are winning

The appeal of mid-century and retro aesthetics is a reaction to something specific: the sameness that has increasingly defined the contemporary interior. When every new café, home, and hotel uses the same five materials — white walls, terrazzo, brushed brass, light oak, linen — spaces stop being interesting. They become settings rather than experiences. Retro design offers a genuine escape from this convergence: a visual language with actual history behind it, one that feels lived-in rather than assembled.

## What retro means for Indian homes

India has its own rich archive of mid-century modernism: the public buildings of Chandigarh, the civic architecture of post-Independence Mumbai, the clean-lined furniture of the 1970s Indian middle class. This design language belongs to us. As the global design conversation rediscovers the power of the past, there is an opportunity for Indian design to reconnect with its own modernist heritage — honest materials, clean geometry, objects made to last rather than to impress for a season.

title: When a room becomes an experience
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
For most of design history, architecture and furniture have been understood as separate disciplines. Architecture defines the shell; furniture fills it. The relationship is sequential and hierarchical — the building comes first, the furniture comes later. A growing body of contemporary design work is disrupting this separation, and the results are some of the most striking interiors being built anywhere in the world. Spanish designer Isern Serra's Barcelona cocktail bar offers a compelling example: modular seating flows continuously across floor, wall, and ceiling, forming a landscape of curved forms that makes the distinction between furniture and architecture essentially meaningless. You don't sit in the room. You inhabit it.

## The experiential interior

What makes this kind of space feel different is its relationship to the body. Standard interior design speaks primarily to the eye — it creates images, compositions, visual effects. Experiential design speaks to the whole body: it changes how you move, how you sit, what you feel when you enter. Indian architecture has always understood this dimension. The cool shadow of a deep veranda. The heightened threshold of a carved doorway. The meditative repetition of a colonnaded courtyard. These are spaces designed to be felt, not just seen.

## Closer to home

You don't need to commission a designer to think experientially about your home. The question is simply: how does this room make you feel when you're in it? Often the answer is not satisfying. And often the fix is not expensive — a change in where the light falls, a rug that defines where you actually spend time, a chair placed at an angle that invites conversation rather than facing the television. Small interventions, experiential effects.

title: The jugaad home — why India deserves purpose-built design
author: Urban Nest Editorial
content:
There is a word in Hindi that captures something essential about how Indian homes actually function: jugaad. A clever improvisation born of necessity. An ice cream container repurposed as a butter dish. A plate used as a cutting surface. A plastic bag serving as a bathroom bin. Jugaad is celebrated in Indian culture as resourcefulness — a tribute to ingenuity. But in the context of the home, jugaad has a cost.

## What improvisation actually looks like

When every object in your home is a compromise — used for a purpose it was not designed for, placed where it fits rather than where it belongs — the cumulative effect is a space that feels perpetually provisional. A home waiting to become a home. This is the experience of millions of Indian middle-class households: not poverty, not affluence, but a persistent gap between the home they want and the products available to create it.

## The gap in the market

India's home décor market has a peculiar structure. At the top: luxury brands offering beautifully designed objects at prices that exclude the majority. At the bottom: functional items that fill the gap without resolving it. The middle — coordinated, design-led, functional accessories at genuinely accessible price points — has been largely absent. Global benchmarks like IKEA and MUJI demonstrate that design-led functionality can transform middle-class living standards; yet their reach in India remains limited and largely furniture-oriented. No Indian brand currently offers a cohesive home accessory experience for middle-income households. That is the gap Urban Nest intends to fill.

## What purpose-built actually means

A bathroom set designed to work together: matching tray, soap dispenser, toothbrush holder, bin, in a consistent material and tone. A kitchen with a chopping board that earns its counter space, a butter dish that replaces the ice cream container, a utensil organiser that makes cooking feel considered rather than improvised. These are not luxury items. They are objects designed for their purpose, made well, and priced for the people who actually need them. The jugaad instinct is honourable. But design should make it unnecessary — not by being expensive, but by being thoughtful. That is what Urban Nest is building.
